source-ref: Alan ruling 2026-06-24, held dark until the first death

content.rule: THE LOOP: dying returns Alan to the floor-1 entrance, staged exactly as the very first scene was, and that symmetry is the reveal. RETAINED across a death: all memory; character level, attributes, skills, titles, affinities and class progress; the HP, Focus and Stamina maxes. LOST: equipment, consumables and anything carried, which belonged to that run of the world. Companions reset and do not remember him; he remembers them. The tower regenerates with enemies respawned and the layout shifted enough that memorisation alone is not the answer, and the upper floors scale, so retained power plus foreknowledge is a real head start rather than a stroll.
content.implications: Alan does not know the loop exists until he dies. Zero foreshadowing: no winks, no asking whether he is sure, no save-point language, and the first death plays completely straight, because for all he knows in the moment he lost. Every design settled from now must stay consistent with the loop so that the reveal contradicts nothing already said. The game master does not engineer a death; play decides when it comes, and the reveal waits as long as it waits. Once the loop is understood it becomes a tool: die to reset, climb again faster and stronger, and push higher than before. The companion reset is revisitable once companions exist and the loop is out.

source-ref: Alan ruling 2026-06-24, the whole-tower escalation mandate

content.rule: THE TOWER ESCALATES. Every floor is measured on two counts and should advance on both, and may regress on neither. NOVELTY: each floor opens a tactical demand no earlier floor made — the first was a chokepoint, then water, then acoustics, then dark and height and timing, then trust and verification. MAGNITUDE: later floors are genuinely bigger and harder rather than only different — more rooms and more interacting systems; a mechanic that evolves across the floor rather than one static gimmick; a threat shape that varies from a single warden to a coordinated pair to a staged multi-phase boss; and lethality that grows with the player's own power, so a later boss carries a real risk of killing rather than a longer bar.
content.implications: The seductive default is scout, then light or solve, then one boss undone by its readable weakness. That was right for the first four floors and is to be broken deliberately from the fifth: multi-phase bosses, puzzles of identification rather than placement, encounters with more than one threat, climaxes carried by the floor itself, staged objectives. Reading beating brute force stays the spine; the shape around it keeps changing. Every floor's lethality is calibrated against the player's sheet as it stands when the floor is written, and every escalation is verified against the mechanics rather than asserted in prose. Each floor leaves the next a clear step: what demand is still unused, and where the size should go.

source-ref: ratified tower-wide 2026-06-24, from the floor-5 ruling

content.rule: A kill of a true form is permanent. A retreat from an enemy only wounded returns that enemy to full when the player comes back. Permanence is counted per enemy rather than per floor: a floor of three wardens where one is killed and the player flees keeps that one dead and returns the other two. What the player keeps across a retreat is everything learned — the tells, the reads, the layout — and what the player loses is the damage dealt to anything not finished.
content.implications: This closes the grind of chipping an enemy down across rests, and makes a floor's real gate whether a true form can be killed in one sustained push. The asymmetry is what makes it read as fair rather than punishing: it rewards the push and the learning and denies only the attrition. The fiction of the recovery varies by floor. An illusion or a construct re-weaves to pristine at once, owing nothing to how long the player was gone. Something physical or living recovers by resting, and the heal has to be carried by time genuinely passing: a breather at the threshold is a partial recovery at most, and only a long rest is a full one. On a physical floor the player's own recovery and the enemy's run off one clock, so the player cannot buy a full restore without granting the enemy the same, and half-resting buys neither. An illusion floor decouples this deliberately, which is why its reset feels eerie where the physical one feels fair. The rule and the per-enemy permanence are fixed tower-wide; the flavour of a recovery and the guardrail on a physical reset may be amended for a floor whose fiction needs it, noted where that floor is written.
